name: Yalarnnga
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Breen, Gavan & Barry J. Blake. 2007. The grammar of Yalarnnga: a language of western Queensland. Pacific Linguistics 584
earlier_scan.note: Full grammar exists (Wikipedia phonology tables note unstressed-position allophones); PDF not reachable

new_statements.quote: Primary stress, heard as greater loudness, fell regularly on the first vowel of a word and a secondary stress was irregularly heard on the third syllable of a four-syllable word or the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme. Further secondary stresses may be heard later in a long word, two or more syllables after the previous stress and not on the final syllable. Some examples, with morpheme boundaries shown by hyphens and stresses by acute (primary) and grave (secondary) accents, are: yírri ‘man’, mángurru ‘dog’, pírlapirla ‘child’, ngálangà-ma ‘speaks’, yálarnnga-ya ‘in Yalarnnga’, wámarrì-yu ‘snake (ergative)’, pínka-yàma-ma ‘scratching oneself’, wántha-ma-nhàti ‘(rain) falling this way’, yúnkunhì-mu-nhàti ‘came back’.
new_statements.citation: Breen, Gavan & Barry J. Blake. 2007. The grammar of Yalarnnga: a language of western Queensland. Pacific Linguistics 584. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, ANU.

The quoted passage is present verbatim at the head of §2.3 (printed p.11, PDF p.23): 'Primary stress, heard as greater loudness, fell regularly on the first vowel of a word and a secondary stress was irregularly heard on the third syllable of a four-syllable word or the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme. Further second…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of every word. Secondary stress is irregular: typically on the third syllable of a four-syllable word or on the first syllable of a disyllabic bound suffix, with further secondaries at least two syllables after the previous stress and never on the final syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Irregularly heard on the third syllable of a four-syllable word or the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme; further secondaries in long words two or more syllables after the previous stress, never word-final (examples: pínka-yàma-ma, wántha-ma-nhàti, yúnkunhì-mu-nhàti). Morphology-sensitive rather than purely rhythmic.
new_statements.exceptions: 'A number of seemingly random exceptions' attributed to speaker age and lack of practice; one probably genuine exception is reduced stress on pronouns (nhína-ma ngìya 'I'm sitting'), alternatively transfer of that reduced stress to the final syllable of the preceding word (wárrka-niyi-kà nhawa 'you might fall'); also movement of main stress off an initial /yi/ syllable to the next (yimata-ta 'for fish'; yiyarlima heard with stress shift and /yi/+/y/ coalescence).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including suffixes); data are from recordings of the last speakers in the late 1960s-1970s, so the description is impressionistic (stress 'heard as greater loudness') and the authors flag speaker uncertainty.
new_statements.identity_note: Breen & Blake 2007 describe Yalarnnga proper (glottocode yala1262, ISO ylr; older spelling Jalanga/Yallunga/Yelina), based on recordings of the last three speakers (Mick and Lardie Moonlight, Maudie Hayden) from 1967-1979; no dialect division is recognised ('No alternative names are known for the language', p. 2). The scan's prior verdict SOURCE-NAMED-UNREACHABLE is now resolved: the grammar is open access at the ANU repository (handle 1885/146740).

Further secondary stresses may be heard later in a long word, two or more syllables after the previous stress and not on the final syllable. Some examples, with morpheme boundaries shown by hyphens and stresses by acute (primary) and grave (secondary) accents, are: yírri ‘man’, mángurru ‘dog’, pírlapirla ‘child’, ngálangà-ma ‘speaks’, yálarnnga-ya ‘in Yalarnnga’, wámarrì-yu ‘snake (ergative)’, pínka-yàma-ma ‘scratching oneself’, wántha-ma-nhàti ‘(rain) falling this way’, yúnkunhì-mu-nhàti ‘came back’.
sources.note: §2.3 'Stress' (pp. 11-12): primary stress (greater loudness) regularly on the first vowel of the word; secondary stress irregularly on the 3rd syllable of a 4-syllable word or the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme, further secondaries two or more syllables after the previous stress and never on the final syllable; sporadic exceptions (reduced stress on pronouns, stress shift off an initial /yi/ syllable).
Phonology tables note allophones 'in unstressed or lax positions' and 'when stressed'; no statement of stress placement; cites Breen & Blake 2007 as its source.
